docs.t: New Mexico anti-SLAPP — Narrow anti-SLAPP statute: only speech at public hearings or meetings in quasi-judicial proceedings
docs.x: New Mexico anti-SLAPP. Narrow anti-SLAPP statute: only speech at public hearings or meetings in quasi-judicial proceedings: NMSA 1978, § 38-2-9.1 (Laws 2001, ch. 218) covers only actions for money damages based on conduct or speech “in connection with a public hearing or public meeting in a quasi-judicial proceeding” before a tribunal or decision-making body of a political subdivision. A “public meeting in a quasi-judicial proceeding” includes meetings or presentations before state, city, town, or village councils, planning commissions, and review boards or commissions (§ 38-2-9.1(D)). This is not a general public-participation statute like California’s. Section 38-2-9.2 states the legislative findings. (NMSA 1978, §§ 38-2-9.1(A), (D), 38-2-9.2)

docs.t: New Mexico anti-SLAPP — Procedure: a special motion, Rule 12 motion, or summary judgment, heard on a priority basis
docs.x: New Mexico anti-SLAPP. Procedure: a special motion, Rule 12 motion, or summary judgment, heard on a priority basis: A covered action is subject to a special motion to dismiss, a motion for judgment on the pleadings, or a motion for summary judgment, which the court must consider “on a priority or expedited basis.” The statute sets no discovery stay, no burden-shifting test, and no deadline for a hearing. The annotations report that courts apply it only where the speech or conduct was in connection with a qualifying proceeding. Examples: a district-court hearing on a recall petition is judicial, not quasi-judicial (Cordova v. Cline, 2013-NMCA-083). Campaign mailers are not covered (Chandler v. Advance N.M. Now PAC, 2021-NMCA-017). Statements to a federal agency are not covered (Ferebee v. Hume, 2021-NMCA-012). (NMSA 1978, § 38-2-9.1(A); annotations to § 38-2-9.1 (2026 NMSA))

docs.t: New Mexico anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory if the motion is filed within 90 days of the answer and granted
docs.x: New Mexico anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory if the motion is filed within 90 days of the answer and granted: If the defendant raises the statute’s protection as an affirmative defense, and the court grants a motion to dismiss, for judgment on the pleadings, or for summary judgment that was filed within ninety days after the moving party’s answer, the court shall award reasonable attorney fees and costs. If the court finds the special motion or summary-judgment motion frivolous or solely intended to cause delay, it shall award fees and costs to the party prevailing on the motion. The annotations report that fees are a sanction, cover appellate work, and carry no prejudgment interest (Cordova v. Cline, 2021-NMCA-022). (NMSA 1978, § 38-2-9.1(B); annotations (Cordova v. Cline, 2021-NMCA-022))

docs.t: New Mexico anti-SLAPP — Expedited appeal for any party
docs.x: New Mexico anti-SLAPP. Expedited appeal for any party: Any party has a right to an expedited appeal from an order on the special motions, or from the trial court’s failure to rule on an expedited basis. The annotations report that the appeal covers rulings on whether the statute applies (Ferebee v. Hume, 2021-NMCA-012) and is limited to speech-based defenses (Valenzuela v. My Way Holdings, LLC, 2024-NMCA-009). The statute sets no separate appeal deadline, so the general rules apply. (NMSA 1978, § 38-2-9.1(C); annotations)

docs.t: New Mexico anti-SLAPP — Not available in federal court; no UPEPA found
docs.x: New Mexico anti-SLAPP. Not available in federal court; no UPEPA found: Per the annotation, the Tenth Circuit held § 38-2-9.1 procedural and inapplicable in federal diversity cases (Los Lobos Renewable Power, LLC v. Americulture, Inc., 885 F.3d 659 (10th Cir. 2018)). The current NMSA Chapter 38 (compiled November 2026) contains no Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, and the 2026 table of newly enacted sections lists none. 2025 session laws were not separately checked, but a 2025 enactment would normally appear in the current Chapter 38. (Annotation to NMSA 1978, § 38-2-9.2; NMSA Ch. 38 (2026); Laws 2026 new-sections table)

docs.t: Ohio anti-SLAPP — Statute: Ohio’s Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (effective April 9, 2025)
docs.x: Ohio anti-SLAPP. Statute: Ohio’s Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (effective April 9, 2025): Ohio adopted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (UPEPA) as R.C. Chapter 2747 (S.B. 237, 135th General Assembly), effective April 9, 2025. It applies to civil actions filed, and claims asserted, on or after that date. It covers claims based on a person’s (1) communication in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding; (2) communication on an issue under consideration in such a proceeding; or (3) exercise of speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights under the U.S. or Ohio Constitution on a matter of public concern. The General Assembly says it intends substantive immunity from suit, not just immunity from liability. Courts must construe the Act broadly and consider uniformity with other UPEPA states. docs.t: Ohio anti-SLAPP — What the Act does not cover
docs.x: Ohio anti-SLAPP. What the Act does not cover: Exempt: (1) claims against a governmental unit or its employee or agent acting in an official capacity; (2) government enforcement actions to protect against an imminent threat to public health or safety; (3) claims against a person primarily engaged in selling or leasing goods or services when the claim arises from communications about that sale or lease (creative, journalistic, political, and artistic works are not ‘goods or services’); (4) survivorship, bodily-injury, and wrongful-death claims, and statements about them. The responding party bears the burden of proving an exemption applies. (R.C. 2747.01(A)(1), (C); R.C. 2747.04(C)(2))

docs.x: Ohio anti-SLAPP. The court may allow limited, specific discovery needed to meet a burden, may hear unrelated motions or public-safety injunction requests for good cause, and fee motions are not stayed. docs.t: Ohio anti-SLAPP — Standard: three steps; Rule 56-type evidence
docs.x: Ohio anti-SLAPP. Standard: three steps; Rule 56-type evidence: The court considers the pleadings, motion, response, and any evidence usable on summary judgment under Civ.R. 56. It must dismiss with prejudice if (1) the movant shows the claim is based on protected activity; (2) the respondent fails to show an exemption; and (3) either the respondent fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the movant’s right to a ruling for fee purposes; a dismissal with prejudice makes the movant the prevailing party. (R.C. 2747.04(B), (C), (E))

docs.x: Ohio anti-SLAPP. If the motion is denied and the court finds it was frivolous conduct under R.C. 2323.51, the respondent gets its fees and expenses, but only after any appeal affirming the denial. (R.C. 2747.05(A)-(B))

docs.t: Ohio anti-SLAPP — Appeal: denial is a final order; 30 days

The statute gives no corresponding immediate appeal from a grant; a grant that disposes of fewer than all claims is subject to the usual final-order and Civ.R. 54(B) rules. (R.C. 2747.05(C); R.C. 2505.02(B)(9); Civ.R. 54(B))

docs.x: Oklahoma land mine. 30-question caps and a 6-hour, business-hours deposition: Interrogatories and requests for admission are each capped at 30 per party (subparts count separately for interrogatories). docs.t: Oklahoma — Anti-SLAPP motion: 60 days from service, and it freezes discovery
docs.x: Oklahoma land mine. docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Statute: Oklahoma Citizens Participation Act
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Statute: Oklahoma Citizens Participation Act: 12 O.S. §§ 1430-1440, effective November 1, 2014, with exemptions amended in 2022 and 2025. It protects the rights to free speech (communication on a matter of public concern: health or safety, environmental, economic or community well-being, government, public officials or figures, or marketplace goods and services), to petition (broadly defined to include communications in or about judicial, official, legislative, and agency proceedings and efforts to get government to consider an issue), and of association. docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Motion to dismiss: 60 days; discovery stops
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Motion to dismiss: 60 days; discovery stops: A party may move to dismiss a legal action (including a counterclaim or cross-claim) that is based on, relates to, or responds to its protected activity. File within 60 days after service of the legal action; the court may extend for good cause. Filing suspends all discovery until the ruling, except specified and limited discovery the court allows for good cause. (12 O.S. §§ 1431(6), 1432, 1435(B))

docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Hearing within 60 days, ruling within 30
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Hearing within 60 days, ruling within 30: The hearing must be set within 60 days after service of the motion, never later than 90 days (120 days if limited discovery is allowed). The court must rule within 30 days after the hearing, considering the pleadings and affidavits. On request of the movant, it must also issue findings within 30 days on whether the suit was brought to deter protected activity or for an improper purpose. (12 O.S. §§ 1433, 1434(A), 1435(A), 1436)

docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Burden shifting
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Burden shifting: The movant must show by a preponderance that the action is based on, relates to, or responds to protected activity. The claimant then avoids dismissal only by establishing by clear and specific evidence a prima facie case for each essential element. Even so, the court must dismiss if the movant proves each element of a valid defense by a preponderance. (12 O.S. § 1434(B)-(D))

docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Mandatory fees and sanctions
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Mandatory fees and sanctions: On dismissal, the court must award the movant costs, reasonable attorney fees, and other expenses as justice and equity require, and must sanction the claimant enough to deter similar suits. If the motion is frivolous or solely for delay, the court may award the respondent costs and fees. (12 O.S. § 1438)

docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Appeal: denial by inaction is appealable and expedited
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Appeal: denial by inaction is appealable and expedited: If the court does not rule within the 30 days, the motion is denied by operation of law and the movant may appeal. Appellate courts must expedite appeals and writs from orders on the motion or failure to rule. (12 O.S. § 1437)

docs.t: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP — Exemptions
docs.x: Oklahoma anti-SLAPP. Exemptions: Does not apply to enforcement actions by the Attorney General or a district attorney; claims against sellers or lessors over statements arising from sales or leases of goods, services, or insurance aimed at actual or potential customers; bodily injury, wrongful death, or survival claims (and statements about them); Insurance Code or insurance-contract claims; and claims from officer-director, employment, or independent-contractor relationships for misappropriating trade secrets or corporate opportunities or enforcing non-disparagement, noncompete, nondisclosure, or confidentiality agreements. docs.t: Puerto Rico — Criminal appeals run from the date of sentencing
docs.x: Puerto Rico land mine. Criminal appeals run from the date of sentencing: A criminal appeal is due within 30 days after the sentence is pronounced, not after notice. The term is jurisdictional. A timely new-trial or reconsideration motion restarts the 30 days from notice of the order resolving it. Certiorari from a conviction on a guilty plea is also 30 days from the sentence, jurisdictional. (Reglamento TA R. 23(A), 32(A))

docs.t: Puerto Rico — Agency review: 30 days to the Court of Appeals
docs.x: Puerto Rico land mine. Agency review: 30 days to the Court of Appeals: Judicial review of a final agency order or decision goes directly to the Court of Appeals within 30 days (jurisdictional) of archivo en autos of the notice, or of the restarted date after a timely agency reconsideration motion, unless a special law sets a different term. (Reglamento TA R. 57)

docs.t: Puerto Rico — Pro hac vice counsel cannot e-file and must bring local counsel everywhere
docs.x: Puerto Rico land mine. Pro hac vice counsel cannot e-file and must bring local counsel everywhere: A courtesy-admitted lawyer has no SUMAC filing access and must file on paper. The endorsing Puerto Rico lawyer must sign every filing and attend every hearing and deposition unless excused. Budget for full local-counsel participation, not a name on the signature block. (Reglamento TS R. 12(f)(2); Directrices SUMAC § V(3))

docs.t: Puerto Rico — Withdrawal needs leave of court
docs.x: Puerto Rico land mine. Withdrawal needs leave of court: Counsel who has appeared must move in writing to withdraw, give reasons, provide the client’s phone and mailing address, and certify the client was notified. The court may refuse in exceptional cases if a party’s rights would be seriously harmed or the case unduly delayed. (R. Proc. Civ. 9.2)

docs.t: Puerto Rico anti-SLAPP — Status not confirmed from the collected texts
docs.x: Puerto Rico anti-SLAPP. Status not confirmed from the collected texts: The collected Puerto Rico court texts (civil and criminal procedure, evidence, court rules, ethics rules, e-filing guidelines) contain no anti-SLAPP procedure: no special motion to dismiss, no discovery stay, and no fee-shifting rule tied to speech or petitioning. An anti-SLAPP law, if one exists, would be a statute outside these rules. Before telling a client anything, search the Leyes de Puerto Rico Anotadas (LPRA) and the Oficina de Gerencia y Presupuesto virtual library (bvirtualogp.pr.gov) for any enacted law on strategic lawsuits against public participation, and confirm its number, effective date, and procedure. No statute is named here because none could be verified. (None verified; check LPRA and enacted laws (Leyes) for any anti-SLAPP statute)

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Civil appeal (apelación) to the TA
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Certiorari to the TA against interlocutory orders (civil or criminal), protection orders, and judgments on arb
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Rule 52.2(b) says “fecha de notificación”) (Regla 32(C) Reglamento TA; Regla 52.2(b) R. Proc. Civ.). Strict compliance: excusable only for special circumstances explained in the petition. No 60-day government extension.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Certiorari to the TA against final resolutions in jurisdicción voluntaria
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Civ.). Jurisdictional, unless a special law sets another term.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Certiorari to the TA against a guilty-plea conviction
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Certiorari to the TA against a guilty-plea conviction: 30 days from Date the sentence was dictated (mailing date of notice if the defendant was not present) (Regla 32(A) Reglamento TA; Regla 193 R. Proc. Crim.). Jurisdictional. Criminal rules compilation current only to Feb. 2020.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Criminal appeal to the TA
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Proc. Crim.). Jurisdictional. Regla 23 counts from notice to the accused of the ruling; Rule 194 counts a reconsideration ruling from its archivo en autos. Criminal rules compilation current only to Feb. 2020.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Recurso de revisión (final agency decision) to the TA
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Recurso de revisión (final agency decision) to the TA: 30 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of the final order (mailing date if later), or the applicable date after a timely reconsideration (Regla 57 Reglamento TA). docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Recurso de revisión especial (welfare benefits, pro se)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Recurso de revisión especial (welfare benefits, pro se): 30 days from Receipt of the agency’s final order (Regla 67(C) Reglamento TA). Only for self-represented persons challenging welfare-benefit decisions.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Electoral certiorari to the TA (CEE cases)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Electoral certiorari to the TA (CEE cases): 10 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of the TPI judgment (or of the ruling on reconsideration) (Regla 42 Reglamento TA). Jurisdictional. docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Serve the recurso and appendix on the other parties (TA)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Serve the recurso and appendix on the other parties (TA): Within the filing term days from Same trigger as the recurso (Reglas 13(B)(1), 23(B), 33(B) y 58(B)(1) Reglamento TA). Strict compliance. docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Notify the TPI when its case has no electronic record
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Notify the TPI when its case has no electronic record: 72 hours (civil appeal); 48 hours (criminal appeal, certiorari) days from Filing of the recurso (Reglas 14(A), 24(A) y 33(A) Reglamento TA). docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Send the original to the TA after filing on paper at the TPI
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Send the original to the TA after filing on paper at the TPI: 48 hours days from Filing at the TPI Secretaría (Reglas 14(C), 24(B) y 33(A) Reglamento TA). Strict compliance. Only when paper filing is allowed under Regla 2.1.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Supplementary certification of service
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Supplementary certification of service: 48 hours (3 business days in revisión) days from Filing of the recurso (Reglas 15 y 58(B)(4) Reglamento TA). Strict compliance.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Late appendix documents, with leave
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Late appendix documents, with leave: 15 days from Notice of the TA resolution allowing late filing (Reglas 16(E)(2) y 34(E)(2) Reglamento TA). Failure to cure may lead to dismissal.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Notice of intent to reproduce oral evidence
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Notice of intent to reproduce oral evidence: 10 days from Filing of the recurso (Reglas 19(B), 29(B) y 76(A) Reglamento TA). Identify portions, dates and witnesses, and the method proposed.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Motion in the TPI or agency for the re-recording (regrabación)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Motion in the TPI or agency for the re-recording (regrabación): 10 days from Notice of the TA order authorizing reproduction (Regla 76(B) Reglamento TA). Pay the fees with the motion.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Transcript of oral evidence
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Transcript of oral evidence: 30 days from Delivery of the re-recording (Regla 76(C) Reglamento TA). Or the term the TA orders; extendable only for good cause by a reasoned motion. Serve copies within the same term.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Stipulated narrative statement: draft, then negotiation
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Stipulated narrative statement: draft, then negotiation: 30, then 20 days from TA authorization; then service of the draft (Regla 76(D) Reglamento TA). If no agreement, the other side files specific objections.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Supplementary brief after transcript or narrative (civil appeal)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Supplementary brief after transcript or narrative (civil appeal): 30 days from Filing of the transcript or narrative statement (Regla 21 Reglamento TA). Announce it when filing the transcript. The appellee may reply within 30 days.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief, civil appeal (TA)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief, civil appeal (TA): 30 days from Filing of the escrito de apelación; or filing of the reproduced oral evidence if any is brought up (Regla 22 Reglamento TA). May include its own appendix.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Opposition to certiorari (TA)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Opposition to certiorari (TA): 10 days from Notification of the petition (Regla 37(A) Reglamento TA). 25 pages paper / 35 electronic.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Respondent’s brief after the TA issues certiorari
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Respondent’s brief after the TA issues certiorari: 30 days from Notice of issuance of the writ (Regla 39(A) Reglamento TA). Extendable. The petition is the petitioner’s brief.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Opposition brief in administrative revisión
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Opposition brief in administrative revisión: 30 days from Notification of the recurso (Regla 63(A) Reglamento TA). Due from the agency, the official and other parties.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Criminal appellant’s brief; then El Pueblo’s brief
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Criminal appellant’s brief; then El Pueblo’s brief: 30, then 30 days from Elevation of the record; then filing of the appellant’s brief (Regla 28(A), (E) Reglamento TA). Unless the TA orders otherwise.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Response to a motion (TA)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Response to a motion (TA): 10 days from Notification of the motion (Regla 68(B) Reglamento TA). The TA may rule sooner in extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Request for an extension (TA or TS)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Request for an extension (TA or TS): At least 3 business days before the term expires days from Expiration of the term (Regla 72(B) Reglamento TA; Regla 48(b) Reglamento TS). Never available for jurisdictional terms.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Panel review of a single judge’s habeas corpus or mandamus resolution
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Panel review of a single judge’s habeas corpus or mandamus resolution: 10 days from Archivo en autos of the notice of the resolution (Regla 55(H) Reglamento TA).

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Reconsideration of a TPI civil judgment
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Reconsideration of a TPI civil judgment: 15 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of judgment (Regla 47 R. Proc. Civ.). Jurisdictional. Serve the other parties within the same 15 days (strict compliance). Must be specific or it does not interrupt.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Reconsideration of a TPI interlocutory order
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Reconsideration of a TPI interlocutory order: 15 days from Notice of the order (Regla 47 R. Proc. Civ.). Strict compliance.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Reconsideration of a criminal sentence or conviction (TPI)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Reconsideration of a criminal sentence or conviction (TPI): 15 days from Date the sentence was dictated (Regla 194 R. Proc. Crim.). Not extendable. Criminal rules compilation current only to Feb. 2020.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Reconsideration in the TA
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Reconsideration in the TA: 15 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of the TA decision (Regla 84(A) Reglamento TA; Regla 216 R. Proc. Crim.). Not extendable. Suspends the term to go to the TS. Opposition within 10 days. Electoral cases: 10 days under Regla 42.

docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Proc. Civ.). Jurisdictional. 60 days in civil cases where the government is a party.

docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Jurisdictional.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Certiorari to the TS against other TA rulings in discretionary recursos, or TA interlocutory resolutions
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Rule 52.2(b) says “fecha de notificación”) (Regla 20(b)(1) Reglamento TS; Regla 52.2(b) R. Proc. Civ.). Strict compliance. In criminal cases, Rule 217 R. Proc. Crim. calls the 30-day term for certiorari against a TA judgment or final resolution denying certiorari jurisdictional; treat it as jurisdictional.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Direct appeal to the TS (unconstitutionality or conflicting TA decisions)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Direct appeal to the TS (unconstitutionality or conflicting TA decisions): 30 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of the TA judgment (or of the ruling on reconsideration) (Regla 17(a) Reglamento TS). Jurisdictional. 60 days in civil cases where the government is a party.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Notify the TA of a recurso filed in the TS
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Notify the TA of a recurso filed in the TS: 72 hours days from Filing in the TS (Reglas 17(b) y 20(d) Reglamento TS). Strict compliance. Stamped copy without the appendix.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Opposition to certiorari (TS)
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Opposition to certiorari (TS): 10 days from Notification of the petition (Regla 20(l) Reglamento TS). 25 pages.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Briefs in the TS after the writ issues or the appeal is accepted
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Briefs in the TS after the writ issues or the appeal is accepted: 30, then 30 days from Receipt of the Secretaría’s notice that the record was received (Regla 35(c)); then receipt of the petitioner’s or appellant’s brief (Reglas 19, 21 y 33(i) Reglamento TS). Regla 33(i) counts the second 30 days from filing of the other side’s brief; Reglas 19 and 21 from receipt. Use the earlier date.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Reconsideration in the TS
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Reconsideration in the TS: 10 business days days from Date the decision was sent to the parties (Regla 45(a)–(b) Reglamento TS). Jurisdictional; 10 pages; no extensions. A second motion only within 3 business days after notice of the denial.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — Electoral certiorari to the TS
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. Electoral certiorari to the TS: 10 days from Archivo en autos of the copy of the notice of the TA judgment (or of the ruling on reconsideration) (Regla 22(a) Reglamento TS). Jurisdictional. Reconsideration within 3 days. The TS rule still cites the 2011 Electoral Code; the Reglamento TA (Regla 41) refers to it as “Regla 21” of the Reglamento TS.

docs.t: Puerto Rico appeal deadline — TA mandate to the TPI or agency
docs.x: Puerto Rico appellate deadline. TA mandate to the TPI or agency: 10 business days days from The TA decision becoming final and firm (Regla 84(E) Reglamento TA). Since 2025 the TA may send it earlier for cause.

docs.t: Rhode Island — 20 days to appeal, and the Supreme Court cannot extend it
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. 20 days to appeal, and the Supreme Court cannot extend it: A civil notice of appeal, with the $150 filing fee, must be filed in the trial court within 20 days of entry of the judgment, order, or decree (not 30). Only the trial court may extend, for excusable neglect, by no more than 30 days past the original deadline; the Supreme Court has no power to extend the time to appeal. (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 4(a), 20(b))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Post-trial motions are due in 10 days, and only some stop the appeal clock
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Post-trial motions are due in 10 days, and only some stop the appeal clock: Renewed motions for judgment as a matter of law, motions to amend findings, new-trial motions, and motions to alter or amend must be served within 10 days after entry of judgment, and the time cannot be extended. Only those four motions restart the 20-day appeal period. A Rule 60(b) motion does not. (Super.R.Civ.P. 6(b), 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e); Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 4(a))

docs.t: Rhode Island — District Court civil appeals: 2 business days
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. District Court civil appeals: 2 business days: To get a de novo trial in Superior Court after a District Court civil judgment, a party must file a written claim of appeal with the District Court clerk within 2 days after entry of judgment, excluding weekends and legal holidays, and pay the costs, including a $50 attorney’s fee for the other side, at that time. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-12-10)

docs.t: Rhode Island — 12% interest from accrual changes settlement math
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. 12% interest from accrual changes settlement math: Prejudgment interest at 12% a year runs from the date the cause of action accrued and is added by the clerk; post-judgment interest is also 12%, accruing on the prejudgment interest as well. Each year between accrual and judgment adds about 12% of the damages award. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-21-10(a))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Arbitration certificate within 3 days and a 30-day rejection window
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Arbitration certificate within 3 days and a 30-day rejection window: Money cases of $100,000 or less are diverted to court-annexed arbitration. Counsel must file the arbitration certificate within 3 days after the last responsive pleading. Missing the 30-day deadline to file a written rejection (with $300) after the award is filed means judgment enters on the award. (Super. Ct. R. Governing Arbitration of Civil Actions 1(a), (e), 5)

docs.t: Rhode Island — Pro hac vice: 3 cases per 5 years, and local counsel in the room
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Pro hac vice: 3 cases per 5 years, and local counsel in the room: Nonresident lawyers are limited to 3 Rhode Island pro hac vice cases in 5 years unless the Supreme Court waives it, and admission is for ‘special and infrequent’ occasions based on client need. Rhode Island counsel must sign every paper and attend every hearing and trial day, ready to proceed alone, unless excused. (Sup. Ct. Art. II, R. 9(a); Super.R.Civ.P. 85)

docs.t: Rhode Island — Slander has a 1-year statute of limitations
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Slander has a 1-year statute of limitations: Claims for words spoken must be filed within 1 year after the words were spoken. Personal-injury claims get 3 years. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-14(a)-(b))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Uncontested-motion trap: object 3 days before the hearing
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Uncontested-motion trap: object 3 days before the hearing: Motions to amend, compel, for protective orders, to consolidate, to add third parties, for Rule 35 exams, to enlarge time after a deadline, and to assign are granted as a matter of course and never reach the calendar unless a written objection stating particular grounds is served and filed at least 3 days before the hearing. The extra day for electronic service does not apply. (Super.R.Civ.P. 7(b)(3))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Discovery runs on Rhode Island numbers, not federal ones
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Discovery runs on Rhode Island numbers, not federal ones: No initial disclosures. Interrogatory answers and document responses are due in 40 days (a defendant gets 60 days after service of process for document requests), with a 30-interrogatory cap. A plaintiff needs leave to serve interrogatories within 60 days after service of process. Untimely interrogatory objections are waived. Supplemental interrogatory answers are due no later than 30 days before trial. An order compelling discovery can provide for automatic dismissal or default if not obeyed within 30 days. (Super.R.Civ.P. 26, 33(a)-(c), 34(b)(2), 37(a)(4)(A))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Do not plead a dollar amount in injury cases
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Do not plead a dollar amount in injury cases: In actions for personal injury, property damage, or wrongful death, the complaint must not state the amount claimed, only that it is enough for the court’s jurisdiction. (Super.R.Civ.P. 8(a))

docs.t: Rhode Island — Miss the Rule 12A statement and the appeal is conditionally dismissed
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Miss the Rule 12A statement and the appeal is conditionally dismissed: The Rule 12A statement is due 20 days after the appeal is docketed. If it is late, the Clerk enters a conditional dismissal that becomes final unless the statement or an extension motion is filed within 10 days. A late appellee counter-statement or brief leads to a conditional default barring further filings and argument. (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 12A(1)-(2), 18A)

docs.t: Rhode Island — Supreme Court briefs need 9 paper copies within 5 days
docs.x: Rhode Island land mine. Supreme Court briefs need 9 paper copies within 5 days: Even with mandatory e-filing, parties must deliver 9 paper copies of Rule 12A statements and briefs (6 of appendices, writ petitions, reargument petitions, and supporting memoranda) within 5 days after the Clerk accepts the electronic filing. Briefs must be in 14-point Times New Roman, double-spaced, with a signed word-count certification and the Clerk’s ‘Checklist for Filing Briefs’; a brief without the checklist is rejected. (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 16(f), 18(b), (h))

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Statute: R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 9-33 (conditional immunity, not a dismissal framework)
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Statute: R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 9-33 (conditional immunity, not a dismissal framework): Rhode Island’s 1993 anti-SLAPP law makes a party’s exercise of the right of petition or free speech, under the U.S. or Rhode Island constitutions, in connection with a matter of public concern, conditionally immune from civil claims, counterclaims, and cross-claims directed at that activity. Covered activity is defined as any written or oral statement (1) made before or submitted to a legislative, executive, or judicial body or other governmental proceeding, (2) made in connection with an issue under consideration by such a body, or (3) made in connection with an issue of public concern. The legislative findings say such suits should be resolved quickly and at minimum cost to the citizen. (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 9-33-1, 9-33-2(a), (e))

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — The only exception: ‘sham’ petitioning or speech, tested two ways
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. The only exception: ‘sham’ petitioning or speech, tested two ways: Immunity is lost only if the speech or petition is a sham, meaning it is not genuinely aimed at procuring a favorable government action, result, or outcome. It is a sham only if it is BOTH objectively baseless (no reasonable person could realistically expect success in procuring the government action) AND subjectively baseless (an attempt to use the governmental process itself, rather than its outcome, for its own direct effects). The statute’s sham test is framed around petitioning government. How it applies to speech on a public issue that is not aimed at any government body is not answered by the statutory text; check Rhode Island case law. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-33-2(a)(1)-(2))

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Procedure: no special motion form, no deadline, automatic discovery stay
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Procedure: no special motion form, no deadline, automatic discovery stay: Immunity may be raised by an appropriate motion or by other appropriate means under the civil rules. The statute sets no filing deadline and no hearing deadline. Filing a motion asserting the immunity automatically stays all discovery until notice of entry of the order ruling on it. The court may allow specified discovery only on motion, after a hearing, for good cause. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-33-2(b)-(c))

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Fees are mandatory for the winner; damages if the suit was frivolous or meant to harass
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Fees are mandatory for the winner; damages if the suit was frivolous or meant to harass: If the court grants the immunity motion, or the speaker or petitioner ultimately prevails at trial, the court must award costs and reasonable attorney’s fees, including those for the motion and related discovery. The court must also award compensatory damages, and may award punitive damages, if the prevailing party shows the claims were frivolous or brought to harass or otherwise inhibit petitioning or speech. Other remedies remain available. (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-33-2(d))

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Intervention by government and the Attorney General; other protections preserved
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Intervention by government and the Attorney General; other protections preserved: The government agency or subdivision to which the petition or speech was directed, or the Attorney General, may intervene to defend or support the speaker. The chapter does not limit other constitutional, statutory, or common-law protections. (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 9-33-3, 9-33-4)

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Appeal of a denial: the statute is silent
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Appeal of a denial: the statute is silent: Chapter 9-33 has no appeal provision, and a denial of an immunity motion is not among the interlocutory orders made appealable by R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-24-7 (injunctions, receivers, ordered sales, and new-trial orders after a jury trial). Review before final judgment would have to come by petition for certiorari to the Supreme Court under Article I, Rule 13. Whether the Supreme Court routinely grants such review is a case-law question not answered by the collected texts. (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 9-33-2, 9-24-7; Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 13)

docs.t: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP — Currency check
docs.x: Rhode Island anti-SLAPP. Currency check: The legislature’s site shows § 9-33-2 last amended by P.L. 1995, ch. 386, and § 9-33-4 by P.L. 1997, ch. 326. No later amendment (for example, adoption of the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act) appears on the official code site as fetched November 10, 2026. (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 9-33-1 to 9-33-4 (History of Section notes))

docs.t: Rhode Island appeal deadline — Notice of appeal, civil (with $150 fee)
docs.x: Rhode Island appellate deadline. Notice of appeal, civil (with $150 fee): 20 days from Entry of the judgment, order, or decree (set forth and signed by the clerk) (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 4(a), 5(a)). Filed in the trial court. Restarts from entry of an order deciding a timely Rule 50(b), 52(b), or 59 motion. The Supreme Court cannot extend it.

docs.t: Rhode Island appeal deadline — Cross-appeal / other party’s notice of appeal
docs.x: Rhode Island appellate deadline. Cross-appeal / other party’s notice of appeal: 20 days from Filing (or deemed filing) of the first notice of appeal, or the ordinary appeal period if longer (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 4(a)). Whichever period ends later.

docs.t: Rhode Island appeal deadline — Extension of appeal time for excusable neglect
docs.x: Rhode Island appellate deadline. Extension of appeal time for excusable neglect: 30 days from Expiration of the original appeal period (Sup. Ct. Art. I, R. 4(a)). Granted only by the trial court; maximum 30 days.

docs.t: Rhode Island appeal deadline — Rule 50(b), 52(b), or 59 post-trial motion (tolls the appeal period)

docs.t: South Carolina — Filing alone does not commence the action

docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Answers in 30 days, motions on 10 days’ notice, 5 extra days after mail service: The answer is due in 30 days. docs.x: South Carolina land mine. docs.t: South Carolina — Discovery caps you will not see in federal court
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. docs.t: South Carolina — Notice of appeal: serve in 30 days from receipt of written notice of entry, then file within 10 days
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Notice of appeal: serve in 30 days from receipt of written notice of entry, then file within 10 days: In civil cases, the notice of appeal must be served on all respondents within 30 days after receipt of written notice of entry of the order or judgment. Within 10 days after service, file it with the lower court clerk and the appellate clerk, with proof of service, the order, and the $250 fee. A late notice or an unpaid fee means dismissal. No court can extend the notice-of-appeal deadline. (Rules 203(b)(1), 203(d)(1)(B), 203(d)(3), 263(b), SCACR)

docs.t: South Carolina — Post-trial motion deadlines changed in 2026: now 20 days
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. A timely motion stays the appeal time for all parties until receipt of written notice of entry of the order deciding it. Older SC sources and practice guides still say 10 days. docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Rule 60(b) has no catch-all ground: South Carolina’s Rule 60(b) omits the federal ’any other reason that justifies relief’ ground. Grounds (1)-(3) (mistake, new evidence, fraud) carry a hard 1-year limit. (Rule 60(b), SCRCP)

docs.t: South Carolina — Settlements between counsel bind only if in the record or signed
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Settlements between counsel bind only if in the record or signed: An agreement between counsel is enforceable only if it is a consent order or signed stipulation entered in the record, made in open court and noted on the record, or reduced to writing and signed by the parties and their counsel. A handshake or an e-mail exchange is not enough. (Rule 43(k), SCRCP)

docs.t: South Carolina — Appeal stays civil judgments automatically (with exceptions)
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Appeal stays civil judgments automatically (with exceptions): Unlike federal practice, serving a notice of appeal in a civil matter automatically stays the order appealed from. Money judgments, injunctions, family court orders regarding a child or support, ejectment orders, and other listed exceptions are not stayed without supersedeas. Apply to the lower court first. (Rule 241(a), (b), (d)(1), SCACR)

docs.t: South Carolina — Rehearing must be actually received in 15 days, and it frames certiorari
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Rehearing must be actually received in 15 days, and it frames certiorari: A petition for rehearing (limit 15 pages) must be actually received by the appellate court within 15 days after the opinion is filed; mailing it is not enough. A Court of Appeals decision cannot be reviewed by the Supreme Court until rehearing has been decided. The certiorari petition may raise only questions raised in the Court of Appeals and in the rehearing petition. (Rules 221(a), 242(c), 242(d)(1), SCACR)

docs.t: South Carolina — Pro hac vice is not a shortcut: local counsel signs and attends, and you cannot e-file
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Pro hac vice is not a shortcut: local counsel signs and attends, and you cannot e-file: Your SC co-counsel must sign every paper and attend every proceeding unless excused. You cannot register for trial-court e-filing. More than six applications in a calendar year bars further pro hac vice appearances. (Rule 404(f), (i), SCACR; SC Electronic Filing Policies and Guidelines § 3(a)(1))

docs.t: South Carolina — Demand letters: no threats of prosecution or bar complaints
docs.x: South Carolina land mine. Demand letters: no threats of prosecution or bar complaints: South Carolina keeps the old Code rule: a lawyer may not threaten criminal or disciplinary charges solely to gain an advantage in a civil matter. (Rule 4.5, RPC, Rule 407, SCACR)

docs.t: South Carolina anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute in the South Carolina Code
docs.x: South Carolina anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute in the South Carolina Code: South Carolina has no anti-SLAPP law: no special motion to dismiss, no discovery stay, and no fee-shifting tied to speech or petitioning. The suggested cite ’S.C. Code § 15-26-10 et seq.’ does not exist. Title 15 has no Chapter 26 (its chapter list jumps from Chapter 19 to Chapter 27), and the old chapter URL returns 404. (S.C. Code tit. 15 chapter index; Code of Laws searches, scstatehouse.gov (Nov. 10, 2026))

docs.t: South Carolina anti-SLAPP — What a speech defendant can use instead
docs.x: South Carolina anti-SLAPP. What a speech defendant can use instead: Without an anti-SLAPP statute, the tools are an ordinary Rule 12(b)(6) motion (the SC wording is failure ’to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action’), summary judgment under Rule 56, Rule 11 sanctions, and the Frivolous Civil Proceedings Sanctions Act. Under the Act, after a verdict or a dismissal by directed verdict, summary judgment, or JNOV, the prevailing party may move for sanctions against a frivolous claim. The test is what a reasonable attorney would believe, proof is by a preponderance, and the person accused gets notice and 30 days to respond. Unlike anti-SLAPP fee shifting, this does not end the case early and does not shift fees automatically. (Rules 11, 12(b)(6), 56, SCRCP; S.C. Code § 15-36-10(A)(4), (C), (D))

docs.x: South Carolina appellate deadline. docs.x: South Carolina appellate deadline. Order transcript (civil): 10 days from Service of notice of appeal (Rule 207(a)(1), SCACR). 30 days in General Sessions and juvenile appeals.

docs.x: South Carolina appellate deadline. Return to certiorari petition: 30 days from Service of the petition (Rule 242(f), SCACR). Reply due 10 days after service of return.

docs.t: South Dakota — Your action is not commenced until the summons is served
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Your action is not commenced until the summons is served: Filing a complaint does not commence an action or stop the statute of limitations. An action is commenced as to each defendant when that defendant (or a codefendant united in interest) is served with the summons. Delivering the summons to the sheriff of the proper county counts only if service or first publication follows within 60 days. (SDCL 15-6-3, 15-2-30, 15-2-31)

docs.t: South Dakota — No notice of entry, no appeal clock, and the notice of appeal can’t be extended
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. No notice of entry, no appeal clock, and the notice of appeal can’t be extended: The 30-day appeal time runs only after the judgment is signed, attested, and filed and written notice of entry is given to the adverse party. A notice of entry not filed within 10 days after service is deemed served on its filing date. The Supreme Court cannot enlarge the time to appeal. The notice of appeal is filed in the circuit court, and the clerk must reject it without the docketing statement, proof of service and filing fee. (SDCL 15-26A-6, 15-26A-4(4), 15-26A-92, 15-6-5(d))

docs.t: South Dakota — Post-trial motions: 10 days, and a 20-day deemed denial
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Post-trial motions: 10 days, and a 20-day deemed denial: Renewed JMOL and new-trial motions are due 10 days after notice of entry of judgment. If the court does not rule, or extend its time by order, within 20 days after the new-trial motion is served and filed, the motion is deemed denied. The appeal clock then starts on that date with no further notice. (SDCL 15-6-50(b), 15-6-59(b), 15-26A-6)

docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Defending the judgment in the brief is not enough. (SDCL 15-26A-22)

docs.t: South Dakota — Order the transcript within 10 days or lose it
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Order the transcript within 10 days or lose it: The appellant must order the transcript on the Supreme Court form within 10 days after filing the notice of appeal, serving the order and filing a copy. Late ordering waives the transcript. (SDCL 15-26A-48, 15-26A-49)

docs.t: South Dakota — Interlocutory review: 10 days from notice of entry
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Interlocutory review: 10 days from notice of entry: Most pretrial orders are reviewable only by a petition for permission to appeal. File it with the Supreme Court within 10 days after notice of entry of the order, with a 10-page limit and required attachments. The petition does not stay the case. (SDCL 15-26A-3(6), 15-26A-13 to 15-26A-15, 15-26A-19)

docs.t: South Dakota — Short-time periods skip weekends; e-service after midnight slips a day
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Short-time periods skip weekends; e-service after midnight slips a day: For periods under 11 days, intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays are excluded. Three days are added only for mail service, not e-mail or fax. Service by e-mail, fax or Odyssey must be completed by 11:59 p.m. Central time on a non-holiday weekday, or it is deemed made the next weekday. Motions must be served at least 10 days before the hearing, responses 5 days before, and replies 2 days before. (SDCL 15-6-6(a), (d), (e))

docs.t: South Dakota — Summary judgment runs on a 28/14/7-day clock with numbered fact statements
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Summary judgment runs on a 28/14/7-day clock with numbered fact statements: The motion, brief, statement of undisputed material facts and affidavits must be served at least 28 calendar days before the hearing, the response at least 14, and the reply at least 7. The opponent must answer each numbered fact with record citations. Facts not controverted are admitted. (SDCL 15-6-56(c))

docs.t: South Dakota — Answer in 30 days, but jury demand in 10
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Answer in 30 days, but jury demand in 10: The answer is due 30 days after service of the complaint, not 21 as in federal court. A jury demand must be served no later than 10 days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue, or the jury is waived. (SDCL 15-6-12(a), 15-6-38(b), (d))

docs.t: South Dakota — Pro hac vice requires a sales tax license and local counsel at trial
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Pro hac vice requires a sales tax license and local counsel at trial: The out-of-state lawyer’s sworn motion must confirm a South Dakota Sales and Use Tax License (or an application for one), unless the lawyer appears for a full-time employer without extra pay. The resident lawyer must personally participate in the trial or hearing, and only South Dakota-admitted active lawyers can issue subpoenas. (SDCL 16-18-2, 15-6-45; S.D. R. Prof. Conduct 5.5(c)(5))

docs.t: South Dakota — Change of judge: ask informally first, and don’t argue anything
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Change of judge: ask informally first, and don’t argue anything: The affidavit for change of judge must be preceded by an informal request to the judge. Submitting argument or proof to that judge on any motion waives the right for the rest of the case. The deadline before a jury trial is 15 days. (SDCL 15-12-21.1, 15-12-24, 15-12-27)

docs.t: South Dakota — Costs waived after 30 days; fee motions due in 14
docs.x: South Dakota land mine. Costs waived after 30 days; fee motions due in 14: Costs are waived unless a verified application is filed within 30 days after entry of judgment, and objections to costs are due within 10 days after service. A motion for attorney fees is due 14 days after entry of judgment. Appellate attorney fees must be sought by motion with a verified itemized statement before the appeal is submitted. (SDCL 15-6-54(d), 15-26A-87.3)

docs.t: South Dakota anti-SLAPP — New anti-SLAPP law: SDCL ch. 15-40 (2026)
docs.x: South Dakota anti-SLAPP. New anti-SLAPP law: SDCL ch. 15-40 (2026): South Dakota enacted its first anti-SLAPP statute in 2026 (SL 2026, ch 91), codified as SDCL ch. 15-40, “Expedited Procedure for SLAPPs.” The text follows the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act model. The codified text does not state an effective date. Before relying on it for conduct or suits that predate the Act, confirm when it took effect and whether it applies to pending cases. (SDCL 15-40-1 to 15-40-13; SL 2026, ch 91)

docs.t: South Dakota anti-SLAPP — Scope: protected public expression
docs.x: South Dakota anti-SLAPP. Scope: protected public expression: The chapter covers a cause of action based on a person’s: (1) communication in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative or other governmental proceeding; (2) communication on an issue under consideration or review in such a proceeding; or (3) exercise of free speech, press, assembly, petition or association rights under the U.S. or South Dakota Constitution on a matter of public concern. It does not apply to claims against government units or employees acting in an official capacity, to government enforcement actions against an imminent threat to public health or safety, or to claims against a seller or lessor of goods or services arising from communications about that sale or lease. docs.t: South Dakota anti-SLAPP — Procedure: 60-day motion, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling
docs.x: South Dakota anti-SLAPP. Procedure: 60-day motion, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling: File a special motion for expedited relief within 60 days after service of the pleading asserting the claim, or later for good cause. Filing stays all other proceedings between the movant and the respondent, including discovery, until the motion is decided and the time to appeal expires. The court may allow limited discovery if specific information is needed and not otherwise available. The court must hear the motion within 60 days after filing (later only for limited discovery or good cause) and rule within 60 days after the hearing. Unrelated motions, public-safety injunctions, fee motions, voluntary dismissals and severance are not stayed. (SDCL 15-40-3, 15-40-4, 15-40-5, 15-40-6, 15-40-7, 15-40-10)

docs.t: South Dakota anti-SLAPP — Standard: dismissal with prejudice
docs.x: South Dakota anti-SLAPP. Standard: dismissal with prejudice: The court considers the pleadings, motion papers and any evidence admissible on summary judgment. It must dismiss with prejudice if: the movant shows the chapter applies; the respondent fails to show an exclusion; and either the respondent fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the motion or the fee claim, and a voluntary dismissal with prejudice means the movant prevailed. (SDCL 15-40-8, 15-40-9)

docs.t: South Dakota anti-SLAPP — Mandatory fees and immediate appeal
docs.x: South Dakota anti-SLAPP. Mandatory fees and immediate appeal: A prevailing movant must be awarded court costs, reasonable attorney fees and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion. A prevailing respondent gets them only if the court finds the motion frivolous or filed solely to delay. A movant may appeal an order denying the motion in whole or in part as of right, within 30 days after entry of the order, and an appeal stays all proceedings between all parties until it ends. (SDCL 15-40-11, 15-40-12, 15-40-4)

docs.t: South Dakota appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (with docketing statement, proof of service, fee) in the circuit court

docs.x: Utah anti-SLAPP. Procedure: 60 days to file, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling: File a special motion for expedited relief within 60 days after service of the pleading asserting the claim, or later for good cause. docs.t: Utah anti-SLAPP — Standard: dismissal with prejudice
docs.x: Utah anti-SLAPP. Standard: dismissal with prejudice: The court considers the pleadings, motion papers, and evidence admissible on summary judgment. It must dismiss with prejudice if the movant shows the Act applies, the responding party fails to show an exclusion, and either the responding party fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the motion or fees; a dismissal with prejudice makes the movant the prevailing party. (Utah Code §§ 78B-25-106, -107)

(Utah Code § 78B-25-110)

docs.t: Virginia — Post-trial motions do not extend the 21-day finality window or the 30-day appeal clock
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Post-trial motions do not extend the 21-day finality window or the 30-day appeal clock: A final judgment leaves the trial court’s control 21 days after the judge signs it. Filing a motion for a new trial or reconsideration does not extend that time or the time to note an appeal. Only an order that actually modifies, vacates or suspends the judgment within the 21 days does, and appeal time then runs from the new final judgment. Get a suspending order entered, not just a motion filed. (Rule 1:1(a); Rule 5A:3(a))

docs.t: Virginia — Notice of appeal goes to the trial court clerk within 30 days, with the $50 fee and an appeal bond
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Notice of appeal goes to the trial court clerk within 30 days, with the $50 fee and an appeal bond: The notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals must be filed with the clerk of the circuit court within 30 days after entry of the final judgment. A copy goes to the Court of Appeals clerk with the $50 fee (the appeal is dismissed if the fee does not arrive within 10 days). In an appeal of right in a civil case, a $500 appeal bond (or the amount the trial court sets) must be filed simultaneously. The bond is not jurisdictional, but missing it invites a motion. (Rule 5A:6(a), (c); Va. Code §§ 8.01-675.3, 8.01-676.1(A), (P))

docs.t: Virginia — Transcripts are due in the trial court within 60 days of judgment
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Transcripts are due in the trial court within 60 days of judgment: A transcript becomes part of the record only if filed in the circuit court clerk’s office within 60 days after entry of final judgment. The Court of Appeals can extend that only on a written motion filed within 90 days after entry. Notice of filing the transcript is due to all counsel within 10 days. Without needed transcripts, the assignments of error may not be reachable. (Rule 5A:8(a)–(b))

docs.t: Virginia — Preliminary assignments of error are due 15 days after the record is filed
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Preliminary assignments of error are due 15 days after the record is filed: In an appeal of right, the appellant must file a preliminary statement of assignments of error within 15 days after the record is filed in the Court of Appeals, and the appellee files any preliminary assignments of cross-error within 10 days after that. The opening brief is due 40 days after the record is filed. Assignments of error must point to exact record pages where each error was preserved; a bare “contrary to the law and the evidence” assignment is insufficient. (Rules 5A:19(b)(1)–(2), 5A:20, 5A:18)

docs.t: Virginia — Preserve every objection with reasonable certainty at the time of the ruling
docs.x: Virginia land mine. A general statement that the judgment is contrary to the law and the evidence preserves nothing. (Rule 5A:18; Rule 5:25)

docs.x: Virginia land mine. Pro hac vice papers are invalid without local counsel’s signature: Any pleading or paper that must be served, including discovery, is invalid unless signed by Virginia local counsel. Local counsel must personally attend every proceeding. The first pleading in a court of record must give a Virginia State Bar number, and a signature by anyone other than an active VSB member or pro se party is not valid. A signature defect must be cured within 21 days after it is raised, or the paper is stricken. (Rule 1A:4(2); Va. Code § 8.01-271.1(A), (G))

docs.t: Virginia — No summary judgment on discovery depositions
docs.x: Virginia land mine. No summary judgment on discovery depositions: A motion for summary judgment or to strike the evidence cannot be sustained if based in whole or in part on discovery depositions under Rule 4:5. The exceptions are all parties agreeing, or the motion coming within § 8.01-420(B)–(C), which allows depositions and affidavits when the only parties are business entities and $50,000 or more is at issue. Summary judgment is decided on the pleadings, pretrial orders and admissions. (Rule 3:20; Va. Code § 8.01-420)

docs.t: Virginia — Answer in 21 days, no general denial, no serial motions
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Answers must respond paragraph by paragraph. After the first response, further demurrers, pleas or motions need leave of court. docs.x: Virginia land mine. Leave to amend from the bench starts a 21-day clock that can end the case: There is no amendment as of right. docs.t: Virginia — Fee claims must be pleaded
docs.x: Virginia land mine. docs.t: Virginia — Nonsuit is a right, but only once and only before submission
docs.x: Virginia land mine. Nonsuit is a right, but only once and only before submission: A plaintiff may take one nonsuit as of right before a motion to strike is sustained, the jury retires, or the case is submitted to the court. The plaintiff may then refile within six months or the remaining limitations period, whichever is longer, generally in the same court. Code §§ 8.01-380(A)–(D), 8.01-229(E)(3))

docs.t: Virginia anti-SLAPP — No special motion, no discovery stay, no statutory deadline
docs.x: Virginia anti-SLAPP. No special motion, no discovery stay, no statutory deadline: The statute sets out no special motion to strike, no filing deadline, no automatic stay of discovery, and no expedited hearing. The immunity has to be raised through ordinary Virginia procedure, for example a demurrer, plea in bar, or summary-judgment motion (Rules 3:8, 3:20), or a motion to quash a subpoena. docs.t: Virginia anti-SLAPP — Fees: discretionary award to the prevailing defendant or witness
docs.x: Virginia anti-SLAPP. The award is discretionary, not mandatory. Under Rule 3:25, a fee claim generally has to be demanded in a pleading; whether that rule reaches a defendant’s § 8.01-223.2 fee request was not resolved from the collected text, so plead it. (Va. Code § 8.01-223.2(C); Rule 3:25)

docs.t: Vermont anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory for a winning defendant; two-way for frivolous motions
docs.x: Vermont anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory for a winning defendant; two-way for frivolous motions: If the motion is granted, the court must award costs and reasonable attorney’s fees to the defendant. If the motion is denied and the court finds it frivolous or meant only to cause delay, the court must award costs and fees to the plaintiff. Separately, 12 V.S.A. § 5771 lets the court award costs and fees to a defendant who wins a defamation action that it finds frivolous and without merit. (12 V.S.A. § 1041(f)(1); 12 V.S.A. § 5771)

docs.t: Vermont anti-SLAPP — Appeal; exclusions
docs.x: Vermont anti-SLAPP. Appeal; exclusions: An order granting or denying the motion is appealable in the same manner as an interlocutory order under V.R.A.P. 5. The statute does not say more. Check whether the appellate courts treat this as an appeal as of right or one that still requires the V.R.A.P. 5 permission procedure; case law was not collected. The statute does not apply to (1) enforcement actions or criminal proceedings brought by the State or a political subdivision, or (2) cases of tortious interference with legally protected health care under 12 V.S.A. § 7302. (12 V.S.A. § 1041(g), (h))

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil, and most agency appeals)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil, and most agency appeals): 30 days from entry of the judgment or order (V.R.A.P. 4(a)(1); 12 V.S.A. § 2383). File with the superior court clerk or agency. Jurisdictional (2026 VT 13, ¶ 4).

docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. State’s notice of appeal in a criminal case: 7 days from entry of the judgment or order (business days) (V.R.A.P. 4(a)(2)). Counted in business days. 30 days if the sentence is life imprisonment and the defendant has not waived appeal.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Cross-appeal / other party’s notice
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Cross-appeal / other party’s notice: 14 days from filing of the first notice of appeal (or the normal period, whichever ends later) (V.R.A.P. 4(a)(6)). File in the superior court.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Motion to extend time to appeal
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Motion to extend time to appeal: 30 days from expiration of the original appeal period (V.R.A.P. 4(d)). Excusable neglect or good cause. Extension capped at the later of 30 days past the original deadline or 14 days after the order.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Motion to reopen time to appeal (no notice of entry)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Motion to reopen time to appeal (no notice of entry): 90 days from entry of judgment (or 14 days after receiving notice, if earlier) (V.R.A.P. 4(c)). Civil only. Notice not received within 21 days. Reopened period is 14 days.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Rule 60 motion that tolls the appeal period
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Rule 60 motion that tolls the appeal period: 28 days from entry of judgment (V.R.A.P. 4(b)(7)). A Rule 60(b) motion attacking a default judgment need only be timely under that rule.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Docketing statement (appellant)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Docketing statement (appellant): 14 days from filing of the notice of appeal (V.R.A.P. 3(e)). Filed in the Supreme Court. The appellee may file one within 14 days after the appellant’s.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Order transcripts
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Order transcripts: 14 days from filing of the notice of appeal (V.R.A.P. 10(b)(1)). At filing of the notice in bail appeals and juvenile abuse/neglect cases (10(b)(4)).

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Appellant’s principal brief and printed case
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Appellant’s principal brief and printed case: 40 days from notice that the record is complete (V.R.A.P. 31(a)(1); 30(e)). 40 days since Sept. 6, 2022 (formerly 30).

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief (and any supplemental printed case)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief (and any supplemental printed case): 30 days from service of the appellant’s brief (V.R.A.P. 31(a)(2); 30(e)). Formerly 21 days. The Court’s timeline says ‘after appellant’s brief is filed.’

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Reply brief: 21 days from service of the appellee’s brief (V.R.A.P. 31(a)(3)). Formerly 14 days.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Response to a motion
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Response to a motion: 14 days from service of the motion (V.R.A.P. 27(a)(3)). Reply to a response on a substantive motion: 7 days (Court guidance).

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Motion for permission to appeal an interlocutory order (trial court)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Motion for permission to appeal an interlocutory order (trial court): 14 days from entry of the order or ruling (V.R.A.P. 5(b)(5)(A); 5.1(a)(2)). State in criminal cases: 7 business days.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Motion for permission to appeal in the Supreme Court after denial
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Motion for permission to appeal in the Supreme Court after denial: 14 days from entry of the trial court’s denial (V.R.A.P. 5(b)(7)(A); 5.1(b)(2); 6(a)(4)). Responses due 14 days after service.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Entry fee after an interlocutory appeal is accepted
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Entry fee after an interlocutory appeal is accepted: 14 days from entry of the order accepting the appeal (V.R.A.P. 5(a)(3), 5(b)(6)(B), 5.1(b)(5)).

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Motion for reargument
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Motion for reargument: 14 days from entry of judgment (V.R.A.P. 40). From the Court’s timeline; rule text not collected.

docs.t: Vermont appeal deadline — Correct a rejected e-filing (keep original filing date)
docs.x: Vermont appellate deadline. Correct a rejected e-filing (keep original filing date): 7 days from notice of rejection or failed submission (2020 V.R.E.F. 5(d)(4)–(5), 5(e)(4)). Appeal of a rejection to the Court Administrator: 7 days; tolls the correction period.

docs.t: Wisconsin — Filing commences the case, but you have 90 days to serve, and that cannot be extended
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Filing commences the case, but you have 90 days to serve, and that cannot be extended: An action is commenced when the summons and complaint are filed, but only if an authenticated copy is served within 90 days after filing. The court cannot enlarge the 90 days. Service must be made with reasonable diligence; substitute service at the home and publication are allowed only after reasonable diligence fails at personal service. (Wis. Stat. §§ 801.02(1), 801.15(2)(a), 801.11(1))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Answer deadline is 20 days, or 45 days in tort, insurer, and state cases
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Answer deadline is 20 days, or 45 days in tort, insurer, and state cases: An answer is due 20 days after service of the complaint, but 45 days if any claim sounds in tort, if an insurance company is a defendant, or if the defendant is the state. The summons must state the correct period (20 or 45 days; 40 days after first publication if served by publication). The same 45-day rule applies to replies, motions to strike, and responses to amended pleadings. (Wis. Stat. §§ 801.09(2), 802.06(1), (6), 802.09(1))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Do not plead a dollar amount in a tort complaint
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Do not plead a dollar amount in a tort complaint: In a tort claim for money, the demand for judgment may not state the amount sought. You must disclose the amount to the court and other parties before a hearing on summary judgment or judgment on the pleadings, and before default or final judgment. (Wis. Stat. §§ 802.02(1m), 802.06(3), 802.08(2), 806.01(1)(c), 806.02(2))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Time computation: periods under 11 days skip weekends and holidays
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Time computation: periods under 11 days skip weekends and holidays: Exclude Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays (including a full day on Good Friday) when a period is less than 11 days. Add 3 days for mail service. Add 1 day for fax, email, or e-filing service only if completed between 5 p.m. and midnight. Late motions to enlarge need excusable neglect, and the court cannot extend the time to appeal, to decide post-verdict motions, or to move under s. 805.17(3) or s. 806.07. (Wis. Stat. § 801.15(1)-(2), (5))

docs.t: Wisconsin — 60-day window to substitute the judge
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. 60-day window to substitute the judge: The peremptory substitution request must be filed within 60 days (plaintiff: from filing; others: from service) and before any preliminary contested matter is heard. Arguing a contested motion first forfeits it. (Wis. Stat. § 801.58(1))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Summary judgment within 8 months, and amend once within 6 months
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Summary judgment within 8 months, and amend once within 6 months: Absent a scheduling order, a summary judgment motion must be made within 8 months after the summons and complaint are filed, served at least 20 days before the hearing, with opposing affidavits at least 5 days before. A pleading may be amended once as of course only within 6 months after filing, and a third-party complaint may be served without leave only within 6 months. (Wis. Stat. §§ 802.08(1)-(2), 802.09(1), 803.05(1))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Discovery has hard caps and no initial disclosures
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Discovery has hard caps and no initial disclosures: Limits absent stipulation or order: 25 interrogatories including subparts; 10 depositions of no more than 7 hours each; document requests reaching back no more than 5 years before the claim accrued. There is no general initial-disclosure rule, but litigation-funding agreements must be produced unprompted. A motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, for judgment on the pleadings, or for a more definite statement automatically stays discovery for up to 180 days. (Wis. Stat. §§ 804.08(1)(am), 804.045, 804.09(1), 804.01(2)(bg), 802.06(1)(b))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Jury: demand early, 5/6 verdict, special verdicts
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Jury: demand early, 5/6 verdict, special verdicts: Demand a jury at or before the scheduling or pretrial conference, whichever is first, and pay the fee on the scheduling order’s timetable, or the jury is waived. Five-sixths of the jurors decide, and the same five-sixths must agree on every question needed for a verdict on a claim. Special verdicts are the default. Failing to object at the instruction and verdict conference waives instruction and verdict errors. (Wis. Stat. §§ 805.01(2)-(3), 802.10(3)(e), 805.09(2), 805.12(1), 805.13(3))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Post-verdict motions: 20 days, then deemed denied at 90
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Post-verdict motions: 20 days, then deemed denied at 90: Motions after verdict must be filed and served within 20 days after the verdict unless the court sets a longer time within those 20 days. If not decided within 90 days after the verdict, they are deemed denied and judgment is entered. In bench trials, a motion to amend findings or the judgment is due 20 days after entry of judgment; undecided at 90 days, it is deemed denied and the appeal clock starts 90 days after entry. (Wis. Stat. §§ 805.16(1)-(3), 805.17(3))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Appeal deadline depends on notice of entry: 45 or 90 days, unextendable
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Appeal deadline depends on notice of entry: 45 or 90 days, unextendable: Appeal within 45 days of entry of the final judgment or order if written notice of entry is given within 21 days of entry; otherwise within 90 days. No court can enlarge it. Serving notice of entry within 21 days is how the winner shortens the loser’s time. Nonfinal orders require a petition for leave within 14 days. (Wis. Stat. §§ 808.04(1), 806.06(5), 809.82(2)(b), 809.50(1))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Email service needs written consent unless both sides e-file
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Email service needs written consent unless both sides e-file: Service of papers by email is allowed only if the recipient consented in writing; between registered e-filing users, the system’s notice of activity is service. Self-represented ‘paper parties’ must be served by traditional methods. Documents needing personal service still need it. (Wis. Stat. §§ 801.14(2), 801.18(6)(a)-(c))

docs.t: Wisconsin — Rule 11 safe harbor and a separate frivolous-claims statute
docs.x: Wisconsin land mine. Rule 11 safe harbor and a separate frivolous-claims statute: Sanctions under s. 802.05 have a 21-day safe harbor before filing the motion. Separately, s. 895.044 allows actual fees, on clear and convincing proof, for claims or defenses brought in bad faith or without reasonable basis, also with a 21-day withdrawal window. (Wis. Stat. §§ 802.05(3)(a)1., 895.044(2))

docs.t: Wisconsin anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute in force
docs.x: Wisconsin anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute in force: Wisconsin has no anti-SLAPP law. The statutes certified November 4, 2026 contain no special motion to dismiss for speech or petitioning (ch. 802 has no s. 802.065, and s. 895.69 is the structured-settlement transfer procedure, not an anti-SLAPP provision). The 2025–26 Legislature considered the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (2025 A.B. 701 / S.B. 666), which would have created s. 802.065 and added it to the motion defenses in s. 802.06(2). A.B. 701 passed the Assembly on February 17, 2026, but both bills died in the Senate on March 23, 2026 under Senate Joint Resolution 1. Earlier 2023 bills also were not enacted. What a speech defendant can use instead: a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, which automatically stays discovery for up to 180 days (s. 802.06(1)(b)); the libel retraction-notice rule (s. 895.05(2));

docs.t: Wisconsin anti-SLAPP — Frivolous-claim fees (s. 895.044) are the closest fee tool
docs.x: Wisconsin anti-SLAPP. Frivolous-claim fees (s. 895.044) are the closest fee tool: A party or the party’s lawyer can be liable for actual costs and reasonable attorney fees for commencing, using, or continuing a claim, defense, or appeal that was brought in bad faith solely to harass or maliciously injure, or that the party or lawyer knew or should have known had no reasonable basis in law or equity. The court must find this by clear and convincing evidence. There is a 21-day safe harbor: if the challenged claim is withdrawn or corrected within 21 days after service of the motion, an award is discretionary; if not, the award is mandatory. (Wis. Stat. § 895.044(1)-(2))

docs.x: Wisconsin appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (final judgment or order), notice of entry given: 45 days from Entry of the final judgment or order, if written notice of entry was given within 21 days of entry (Wis. Stat. §§ 808.04(1), 806.06(5)). Jurisdictional; cannot be enlarged (s. 809.82(2)(b)).

docs.t: Wisconsin appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (final judgment or order), no notice of entry
docs.x: Wisconsin appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (final judgment or order), no notice of entry: 90 days from Entry of the final judgment or order (Wis. Stat. § 808.04(1)). Jurisdictional; cannot be enlarged.
